content: The optimal target for glycaemic control in pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes remains uncertain, despite the established association between elevated glucose levels and adverse birth outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of varying intensities of glycaemic control in pregnant women with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Three randomized controlled trials were included, all involving women with type 1 diabetes, encompassing a total of 223 women and their babies. These trials were assessed to have a high risk of bias due to the absence of blinding, unclear randomization methods, and selective outcome reporting. Two trials compared very tight glycaemic control (fasting blood glucose [FBG] levels of 3.33 to 5.0 mmol/L) with tight-to-moderate control (FBG levels of 4.45 to 6.38 mmol/L). In one trial involving 22 babies, no perinatal deaths or serious perinatal morbidity were reported, but the evidence for these outcomes was graded as low quality. In the same trial, two congenital anomalies were observed in the very tight control group, while none were reported in the tight-to-moderate group. There were no significant differences in caesarean section rates between the groups (risk ratio [RR] 0.92, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49 to 1.73), but the evidence for this outcome was graded as very low quality. By the third trimester, glycaemic control was not significantly different between the very tight and tight-to-moderate groups in these two trials. However, one trial involving 22 women found significantly fewer instances of maternal hypoglycaemia in the tight-to-moderate group. A separate trial involving 60 women and their babies compared tight (FBG ≤ 5.6 mmol/L), moderate (FBG 5.6 to 6.7 mmol/L), and loose (FBG 6.7 to 8.9 mmol/L) glycaemic control targets. In this trial, there were two neonatal deaths in the loose control group, while no neonatal deaths occurred in the tight or moderate groups. The evidence for this outcome was graded as very low quality. The combined tight-to-moderate group had significantly fewer cases of pre-eclampsia (evidence graded low), fewer caesarean sections (evidence graded low), and fewer babies with birthweights above the 90th percentile (evidence graded low) compared to the loose control group. The overall quality of evidence for key outcomes was graded as low or very low due to study design limitations, the small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals that crossed the line of no effect. Additionally, many important outcomes were not reported in these studies. In conclusion, the limited evidence available suggests minimal differences in outcomes between very tight and tight-to-moderate glycaemic control targets in pregnant women with pre-existing type 1 diabetes, including the actual glycaemic control achieved. However, there is evidence of harm associated with loose glycaemic control (FBG above 7 mmol/L), including increased rates of pre-eclampsia, caesarean sections, and birthweights above the 90th percentile. Future research should focus on comparing specific interventions rather than glycaemic control targets. Additionally, trials involving pregnant women with pre-existing type 2 diabetes are needed.
